The Jacobite Rising refers to a series of military rebellions primarily from 1645 to 1746 by Scottish Highlanders and their English Catholic allies attempting to restore the Stuart dynasty to the British throne. The term "Jacobite" derives from Jacobus, the Latin form of James, referencing the deposed James II. The final and most famous rising in 1745 to 1746 under Bonnie Prince Charlie resulted in catastrophic defeat at Culloden, ending both Highland military power and the clan system as an independent force.

The Jacobite cause arose from religious conflict. The Stuart kings were Catholic or Catholic-sympathizers in a newly Protestant Britain following the Reformation. The Glorious Revolution in 1688 deposed James II, replacing him with the Protestant William III and his wife Mary. Jacobites viewed this as illegitimate usurpation. Support concentrated in the Scottish Highlands, where the clan system remained strong and loyalty to the Stuarts ran deep. Loyalty to the Crown was personal rather than institutional.

Multiple risings occurred in 1689, 1708, 1715, 1719, and 1745. Each was progressively more desperate and smaller in scale, reflecting declining support and military capacity. The 1745 Rising under Charles Edward Stuart, called Bonnie Prince Charlie, momentarily reached as far south as Derby before retreating. It came closest to succeeding. The decisive defeat at Culloden in 1746 broke Highland military capacity and Scottish independence aspirations for generations. The battle lasted only an hour. Government response was merciless: executions, forfeiture of lands, and systematic dismantling of the clan system followed, with over twelve hundred Jacobites dying at Culloden.

The government banned Highland dress, tartan, and Gaelic language—cultural erasure designed to break Highland identity and prevent future resistance. The aftermath enabled the Highland Clearances, transforming feudal clan tenure into capitalist sheep farming, displacing thousands and depopulating the Highlands.
